title: Hannah, and the Boy Who Heard God
subtitle: 1 Samuel 1
description: Hannah's prayer, a vow kept, and a boy who learns to answer God in the night at Shiloh.
paragraphs: Ruth's story ended in Bethlehem with a genealogy. This book opens a few miles north, in the hill country of Ephraim, in a house divided against itself by love and arithmetic. Elkanah had two wives. Peninnah had children. "And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none", and the text lays the cause where Hannah herself laid it: the LORD had closed her womb. Year after year the family went up to Shiloh to worship the LORD of Hosts at the sanctuary, where Eli the priest served and his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, served as priests. Year after year Elkanah gave Hannah a double portion of the sacrifice, because he loved her, and year after year her rival provoked her viciously over the children she did not have, until she wept and could not eat. Her husband tried to comfort her with the worst comforter's line in the Bible, kind and useless at once: "Am I not better to you than ten sons?"

One year at Shiloh, after the meal, Hannah stood up and went to pray, and what she did in the sanctuary was new enough that the priest misunderstood it completely. She prayed in her heart. Her lips moved and no sound came out, because the prayer was not performance, it was a negotiation conducted in tears: "O LORD of Hosts, if only You will look upon the affliction of Your maidservant and remember me, not forgetting Your maidservant but giving her a son, then I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall ever touch his head." A son for a son. Give me a boy and I will give him back, whole, for life, marked as a Nazirite from birth. Eli, watching her mouth from his chair by the doorpost, concluded she was drunk and rebuked her for bringing wine into the sanctuary, and Hannah's answer has the dignity of a woman who has been misread by everyone: "I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have not had any wine or strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD." And she added: "for all this time I have been praying out of the depth of my anguish and grief." Eli believed her, and blessed her, and sent her away with the words she had come for: "Go in peace," Eli replied, "and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him." She went and ate, and her face was no longer downcast, before a single fact of her life had changed.

The facts changed at home in Ramah. "Elkanah had relations with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her", and she conceived, and bore a son, and named him Samuel, saying, "Because I have asked for him from the LORD." Remembered is one of the Bible's great quiet words; it is what God did for Noah in the ark and for Rachel in her own closed womb, and it never means He had forgotten. It means the waiting turned. But Hannah's vow had a second half, and she kept it with both hands. She did not go up to Shiloh again until the boy was weaned, until she could take him and leave him. Then she brought him, with a bull and flour and wine, to the old priest who had once accused her of drunkenness, and she reintroduced herself by her answered prayer, and gave the boy away in one sentence: "I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him, I now dedicate the boy to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD."

Before she left him there, she prayed again, and this time it came out as a song, and the song is far bigger than her nursery. Hannah sang of a God who reverses everything: "My heart rejoices in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD." "There is no one holy like the LORD. Indeed, there is no one besides You! And there is no Rock like our God." And then the reversals roll: "The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble are equipped with strength." "The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up." "He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor." The barren woman sings it as theology, not just testimony, the whole world's order turned by a God who lifts the low. And at the very end her song does something astonishing. It looks clean past her own story, past Eli, past everything in Israel at that moment, and lands on a figure who does not exist yet: God "will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed." A king. An anointed one. Israel had no king, had not asked for one, and the first mention of God's anointed in this book comes out of the mouth of a formerly barren woman leaving her toddler at the sanctuary. The whole two books of Samuel are inside that line, sung before any of it happened.

At Shiloh, the song's world and the sanctuary's world collided daily, because the boy now lived inside the contrast the rest of the chapters are built on. On one side, Samuel: "the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest", a child in a linen ephod, and each year his mother made him a little robe and brought it up with the annual sacrifice, and the boy grew, in the text's repeated phrase, in the presence of the LORD. On the other side, the priest's own sons, and the text does not hedge: "Now the sons of Eli were wicked men; they had no regard for the LORD". Their racket was the sacrifice itself. A servant ran a three-pronged fork into the boiling pot and the priests kept whatever it brought up, and before the fat was even burned, the fat that belonged to God, they demanded raw meat by threat: give it now, or it will be taken by force. "Thus the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD, for they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt." They were also sleeping with the women who served at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Eli heard all of it. Eli was very old. Eli rebuked them the way tired men rebuke grown sons, with a question and a proverb: "but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?" They did not listen, and the narrator adds, in one of the coldest asides in the book, that they would not listen "since the LORD intended to put them to death."

Judgment, when it came to Eli's house, came first by a stranger. A man of God arrived with a message that reviewed the whole history of the priesthood, the honor of being chosen, and then turned: "You have honored your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of all the offerings of My people Israel." That is the charge against Eli himself, not theft, not lust, but priority: he honored his sons more than God, and fed on the proceeds. The verdict revoked a promise and laid down a principle in its place: "For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained." His house would be cut down, no old men in it, and the sign would be brutally specific: of Hophni and Phinehas, "They will both die on the same day." Inside the same judgment sat a promise the book will spend chapters fulfilling: "Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind. And I will build for him an enduring house, and he will walk before My anointed one for all time." The anointed again. Even the sentence on the old order ends looking at the king to come.

And then, in the middle of that hushed and corrupt sanctuary, God started speaking to the boy. "Now in those days the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were scarce", and the scene is set like a held breath: Eli nearly blind in his room, and Samuel lying down in the temple near the ark of God, before the lamp of God had gone out. Three times the voice called his name, and three times the boy ran to Eli, because he did not yet know the LORD, and three times the old man sent him back. It was Eli, the failing priest under judgment, who finally understood what was happening in his own sanctuary and taught the boy the sentence that would govern his whole life. If He calls you again, Eli said, answer Him: "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening." The fourth time, the LORD came and stood there, and called the name twice, and Samuel answered with a servant's grammar he kept for sixty years: "Speak, for Your servant is listening."

His first message as a prophet was the judgment on the house of the man who had taught him how to answer. God told him the sentence on Eli would be carried out from beginning to end, because Eli knew what his sons did and did not restrain them, and He sealed it with words no boy should have to carry to breakfast: "The iniquity of Eli’s house shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering." Samuel lay awake until morning and opened the doors of the sanctuary as usual and was afraid to speak. Eli made him tell it, all of it, swearing him to hide nothing, and then the old man did the finest thing he does in this book. He heard his own house's death sentence from the lips of a child, and he bowed to it: "He is the LORD," replied Eli. "Let Him do what is good in His eyes."

The word of the LORD had been rare in Israel. By the end of the chapter it had a voice the whole country could name: "And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground. So all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD." But the boy was still serving at Shiloh, in Eli's house, beside Eli's sons, and the sign God had given was both brothers dead on the same day. The Philistines were about to provide the day.

title: The Ark Taken, and Ebenezer
subtitle: 1 Samuel 4
description: The ark carried into battle and captured, Dagon fallen, and a stone of help raised at Mizpah.
paragraphs: The sign God gave Eli's house had a date waiting for it, and the Philistines set it. Israel marched out to fight them and camped at a place called, of all things, Ebenezer, and lost four thousand men in the first battle. The elders' diagnosis of the defeat was theological, and it was wrong in the way that religious confidence can be wrong. "Why has the LORD brought defeat on us before the Philistines today? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh, so that it may go with us to save us from the hand of our enemies." The ark was the throne-footstool of God, the place between the cherubim where He had promised to meet Moses. The elders treated it as a weapon to be carried onto the field, a guarantee that could be hauled out of the sanctuary and pointed at the enemy, and they sent for it, and Hophni and Phinehas, the two priests whose corruption had brought the sentence down, came with it into the camp. Israel shouted so loudly the ground shook.

The shout frightened the Philistines half to death. They knew the old stories, Egypt and the plagues, and they said the gods had come into the Hebrew camp. And then, in one of the most honest moments an enemy gets in this book, fear turned into resolve: "Take courage and be men, O Philistines! Otherwise, you will serve the Hebrews just as they served you. Now be men and fight!" They fought like men who believed surrender was slavery, and Israel, with the ark on the field and the shout still in the air, was routed. Thirty thousand foot soldiers fell. "The ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died." Both brothers, on the same day, exactly as the man of God had said. The ark had not saved Israel. The ark had been taken, because the God of the ark was not a talisman to be carried by corrupt priests into a battle He had not called.

A runner from Benjamin tore through to Shiloh with his clothes ripped and dirt on his head, and found Eli sitting by the road, watching, blind, ninety-eight years old, his heart trembling, the text says, not for his sons but for the ark of God. The report came in stages and each stage was worse, and Eli bore the first ones. Israel had fled. There had been a great slaughter. "Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are both dead, and the ark of God has been captured." At the mention of the ark, not at the mention of his sons, the old man fell backward off his chair by the gate and broke his neck and died, having judged Israel forty years. Down in the town, Phinehas' wife, pregnant, heard the news and went into labor and died giving birth to a son, and with her last strength she named the boy for the whole catastrophe: Ichabod, no glory, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel," because the ark of God had been captured. A dying woman gave the era its epitaph.

What the Philistines did with their trophy tells you what they thought they had won. They carried the ark into the temple of their god Dagon in Ashdod and set it beside his statue, a prisoner of war presented to the victor. In the morning Dagon was on his face on the floor before the ark. They stood him back up. The next morning he was down again, and this time his head and his hands were broken off and lying on the threshold: "Only the torso remained." The text reports this with a perfectly straight face, and notes, almost as an aside, that Dagon's priests in Ashdod do not step on the threshold to this day. Then the hand of the LORD, which Israel had tried to borrow for a battle, fell on Ashdod on its own errand: tumors, panic, a plague with rats in it, and the ark began a tour no one had planned, from Ashdod to Gath to Ekron, and at Ekron the people screamed when it arrived: "They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!" The prisoner was conquering the empire city by city, without one Israelite soldier in the room.

After seven months the Philistines consulted their own priests about how to send it back, and their priests, to their credit, read the situation more clearly than Israel's elders had. Do not send it back empty, they said. Send a guilt offering: five gold tumors and five gold rats, one of each for every Philistine ruler. "Give glory to the God of Israel, and perhaps He will lift His hand from you and your gods and your land." And they reached for the precedent their whole region knew: "Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?" Then they designed a test to settle whether any of this had been God at all. Two milk cows, never yoked, calves taken away and penned, hitched to a new cart with the ark on it and no driver. If the cows walked away from their own crying calves and took the road to Israelite Beth-shemesh, it was the LORD. The cows went straight up the highway, "lowing as they went, never straying to the right or to the left", with the five rulers of the Philistines walking behind to watch their god's conqueror leave. At Beth-shemesh men were harvesting wheat, and they looked up and saw the ark coming driverless into the valley, and the cart was chopped for firewood and the cows offered on a great rock, and the day was joy. But the chapter does not end in joy, because the holiness that had flattened Dagon was not tame for Israel either. Seventy men of Beth-shemesh were struck down for looking inside the ark, and the town asked the question Shiloh should have asked years before: "Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?"

So the ark went to rest at Kiriath-jearim, in the house of Abinadab on the hill, guarded by his consecrated son Eleazar, and there it stayed. And there the story does something quiet and enormous: "And from that day a long time passed, twenty years in all, as the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim. And all the house of Israel mournfully sought the LORD." Twenty years compressed into a verse, twenty years with no ark in any sanctuary, no great prophet's campaign, just a nation slowly mourning its way back toward God. When Samuel finally speaks in this book as its leader, it is at the end of those twenty years, and his first address is not strategy, it is conditions: "If you are returning to the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among you, prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only. And He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines." Israel obeyed. The Baals and Ashtoreths went out, and the nation gathered at Mizpah and poured water out before the LORD and fasted and said the sentence revival always comes down to: "We have sinned against the LORD."

The Philistines heard about the gathering and did what armies do with unarmed revival meetings: they marched on it. Israel panicked, and turned, at last, to the right address: "Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines." Samuel offered a lamb and cried out, and Hannah's song walked off the page: she had sung that God would thunder from heaven against His enemies, and now, as the Philistine line advanced on a praying congregation, "the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel". Israel charged out of Mizpah and pursued them, and afterward Samuel set up a single stone between Mizpah and Shen and gave it the name the first battle's campsite had carried in irony. Ebenezer. "Thus far the LORD has helped us." The first Ebenezer was where Israel tried to use God and lost thirty thousand men and the ark. The second was where Israel gave God back His conditions and won without a battle plan. The stone was the lesson in geography.

The Philistines were subdued, the text says, and did not invade again all the days of Samuel, and the stolen cities came back, and Samuel settled into the work the book opened its adult story with: he judged Israel all his life, riding a yearly circuit, Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah, and home to Ramah, where he built an altar. The boy who had answered a voice in the dark had become the nation's judge, priest, and prophet in one person, and for twenty years and more the system held together on the strength of one faithful man. It was a good system. It had one flaw, and Samuel was mortal, and his sons were already grown.

title: Give Us a King
subtitle: 1 Samuel 8
description: Israel demands a king, Samuel warns what a king will take, and Saul is found among the baggage.
paragraphs: The system that held Israel together for twenty years had the same flaw as the one before it, and it showed up in the same place: the judge's sons. Samuel grew old and appointed his boys, Joel and Abijah, as judges in Beersheba, and the text gives them the epitaph Eli's sons earned a generation earlier, in the vocabulary of the courthouse instead of the sanctuary: "But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice." Twice now a faithful man's household had rotted at the top, and the elders of Israel drew the conclusion that seemed obvious and reached, with it, for the most consequential demand in the nation's history. They came to Samuel at Ramah with a diagnosis and a prescription. The diagnosis was true: "you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways." The prescription was the problem: "Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations."

Samuel took it as a personal rejection and prayed, and God's answer reframed the entire request in one sentence: "Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king." Not a succession plan. A regime change. Since Egypt they had been doing this, God said, forsaking Him for other gods, and now the forsaking had found its final form: they wanted a king of flesh to do what their invisible King had been doing since the Exodus, judging them and fighting their battles. God's instruction was to grant it, but to price it first, solemnly, in public. So Samuel delivered the warning, and the warning is built on one verb, repeated like hammer blows. The king will take. He will take your sons for his chariots and his plowing and his weapons. He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of your grain, a tenth of your flocks, your servants, your cattle, your donkeys, "and you yourselves will become his slaves". And then the line that makes the speech prophecy rather than politics: "When that day comes, you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day."

They heard the whole price list. They said no to the warning itself: "We must have a king over us. Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles." Like all the other nations. Go out before us and fight our battles. Within living memory the LORD had thundered the Philistines off a praying congregation at Mizpah without Israel lifting a sword, and the elders' request was still this: give us a man we can see, to do reliably what God does on His own schedule. God told Samuel to listen to their voice and appoint the king. Judgment and mercy arrive in the same act here, because the man God had already chosen to send was, in God's own words about him, a rescuer: He had looked on His people, and their cry had come to Him. Israel would get its king. Israel would also get exactly the king its request described.

He came from the smallest tribe, the one the other tribes had nearly exterminated in the last chapters of Judges. Kish the Benjamite had a son named Saul, "choice and handsome, without equal among the Israelites", and, in the detail the book will keep using like a measuring stick, "a head taller than any of the people". The future king enters the story herding lost livestock. His father's donkeys had wandered off, and Saul and a servant searched the hills for days and found nothing, and were about to give up when the servant suggested consulting the seer in the nearby town, a man of God whose word always came to pass. He meant Samuel. Saul worried about the gift etiquette, the servant produced a quarter shekel of silver from his own pocket, and Israel's first king walked into his destiny looking for donkeys, carrying somebody else's money, to ask a prophet for directions.

God had spent the previous day preparing the prophet. "At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you are to anoint him ruler over My people Israel; he will save them from the hand of the Philistines. For I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me." When the tall young stranger appeared in the gateway, God named him to Samuel on the spot: "Here is the man of whom I spoke; he shall rule over My people." Saul asked the seer where the seer's house was, and Samuel answered, I am he, and proceeded to unmake Saul's errand piece by piece. The donkeys were found; forget them. The place of honor at the feast was his. The cook brought out a leg of meat that had been set aside on orders before Saul ever left home, and Samuel said it had been kept for this occasion. And Saul, to his credit, pushed back with the truth about himself as he knew it: "Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? So why would you say such a thing to me?" He meant it. Remember that he meant it. The tragedy of Saul is not that his humility was fake at the start; it is what happened to it.

On the roof that night Samuel talked with him, and in the morning, at the edge of the city, he sent the servant ahead and took out a flask of oil and poured it on Saul's head and kissed him: "Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?" Then came the signs, three of them for one day's walk home: men at Rachel's tomb with news of the donkeys, three pilgrims at the Oak of Tabor who would hand him bread, and at Gibeah of God a band of prophets coming down from the high place, at which point the Spirit of the LORD would rush on him and he would prophesy and be turned into another man. It all happened, exactly, in order. The neighbors who saw the donkey-herder ranting with the prophets asked the question that became a proverb on the spot: "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" And when his uncle quizzed him, Saul told him about the donkeys and said not one word about the kingship. Whether that was humility or the first instinct to hide, the text lets it sit there unnamed, the way it let the baggage sit later.

Samuel summoned the nation to Mizpah, the same ground where the thunder had rolled, and before he ran the lot he made them hear what the lot meant. He recited the Exodus, the rescues, the whole record, and then named their day: they had rejected the God who saves them from all their troubles, and had said to Him, "No, set a king over us." Then tribe by tribe, clan by clan, the choice narrowed: Benjamin, the smallest; the clan of Matri; and Saul son of Kish. And Saul could not be found. They inquired of the LORD again, and the answer has embarrassed kingship ever since: "Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage." They ran and fetched him out of the luggage, and stood him up in the crowd, and he was a head taller than anyone there, and Samuel presented him with the people's own criteria satisfied in full view: "Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!" Samuel wrote the rights and duties of kingship on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD, a written constitution for a job they had just been warned about, and everyone went home. Saul went home to Gibeah with a band of men whose hearts God had touched. And some worthless men looked at the tall, silent, baggage-hiding new king and asked the question the Philistines were about to answer: "How can this man save us?" They brought him no gifts. Saul heard about it, and held his peace, and said nothing at all.

title: The Kingdom Renewed, and the First Crack
subtitle: 1 Samuel 11
description: Jabesh rescued, Samuel's farewell, and Saul's unlawful sacrifice at Gilgal.
paragraphs: The test came from across the Jordan, from Ammon. Nahash the Ammonite besieged Jabesh-gilead, an Israelite town in the hills east of the river, and Jabesh offered to surrender and serve him, and Nahash named his price with the cruelty of a man composing an insult to a whole nation: "I will make a treaty with you on one condition, that I may put out everyone’s right eye and bring reproach upon all Israel." Half-blind every fighting man in Jabesh, and let the scar preach Ammon's victory forever. The elders begged seven days to send messengers through Israel, in case a deliverer existed, and Nahash, certain none did, let them. The messengers reached Gibeah, Saul's town, and the people wept, and Saul came in from the field behind his oxen, still a farmer, asking why everyone was crying. They told him. And the Spirit of God rushed on him as it had at Gibeah among the prophets, and he burned with anger, and the new king did something that belonged to the judges' era: he cut a pair of oxen into pieces and sent the pieces through Israel with a threat, march out behind Saul and Samuel or this happens to your oxen. The terror of the LORD fell on the people, and they came out as one man, three hundred thirty thousand of them at Bezek.

Saul's message to Jabesh deserves remembering for its plainness: deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot. Jabesh lied beautifully to buy the night, telling Nahash they would come out in the morning to surrender, and at dawn Saul's army came through the Ammonite camp in three divisions instead, and slaughtered them until the heat of the day, until the survivors were so scattered that "no two of them were left together". Then the nation, drunk on its first royal victory, turned on the men who had sneered at Gibeah and demanded them for execution: "Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Bring those men here so we can kill them!" And here the book gives Saul his finest sentence, the high-water mark of the man, and it is worth weighing because everything later is measured against it: "No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel." The victory was God's, so the vengeance was nobody's. The king who had hidden among the baggage refused a purge and credited heaven. Samuel seized the moment and marched everyone to Gilgal, where the kingship was renewed with sacrifices and great joy, Saul publicly confirmed at last, the question of the worthless men answered by a battlefield instead of a scaffold.

Then Samuel stepped down, and his farewell address at Gilgal is a courtroom and a history lesson and a father's warning folded into one speech. He began with his own audit, an old man inviting prosecution: "Here I am. Bear witness against me before the LORD and before His anointed: Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes? Tell me, and I will restore it to you." The nation cleared him in one voice: "You have not cheated us or oppressed us," they replied, "nor have you taken anything from the hand of man." Against that clean record Samuel recited theirs: Egypt, Moses and Aaron, the forgetting, the sellings into enemy hands, Sisera and the Philistines and Moab, the cries, and the deliverers God sent, Jerubbaal and Barak and Jephthah and Samuel himself, the whole of Judges summarized as one pattern of rescue. And then he attached the pattern to their present: "But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was moving against you, you said to me," and Samuel quoted their demand back at them, "No, we must have a king to rule over us", and added the rider the whole book insists on, that they had said it even though the LORD their God was their king. Nahash had been the trigger. They had asked for a king because an Ammonite was coming, and the Ammonite had just been routed, and the king they got for the asking was now standing beside the prophet who was warning them both. The terms going forward were plain and they were conditional: fear the LORD, serve Him, obey, and it will go well; rebel, and His hand will be against you as it was against your fathers.

To seal it, Samuel did the thing that separated prophecy from oratory. It was wheat harvest, the dry season, when rain does not come. "I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain, so that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king." The thunder rolled in off a harvest sky and the rain fell in the wrong month, and the people stood in it and confessed the exact sin the sign was about: "For we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king." And Samuel, who had every right to say I told you so, pastored them instead. Do not be afraid. Serve the LORD with all your heart anyway. Do not chase worthless things. And then the old man made a promise that defines him as much as any prophecy: "As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. And I will continue to teach you the good and right way." He would pray for the people who had rejected his life's work, and teach them, and he closed with the appeal that outlasts every system: "consider what great things He has done for you." But the warning stayed attached, and it named the king as well as the nation: "But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away."

Time passed. Saul built a standing force of three thousand, two thousand with himself at Michmash and a thousand under his son Jonathan at Gibeah. Jonathan struck the first blow of the reign, attacking the Philistine outpost at Geba, and the war Israel had wanted a king for arrived at full scale: chariots, six thousand horsemen, "and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore", camped at Michmash. Israel's militia melted into the landscape, hiding in caves and thickets and cisterns, and some fled clear across the Jordan. Saul waited at Gilgal for Samuel, bound by the instruction given at his anointing: wait seven days for the prophet to come and offer the sacrifices and give the word. He waited the seven days. Samuel did not come within them, and the troops began to desert, and the Philistine army sat in the pass above him, and Saul did the math of a man watching his command dissolve. He called for the offerings. He offered the burnt offering himself, king doing priest's work, seizing with his own hands the favor he was supposed to wait to receive. "Just as he finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to greet him."

His defense was a list of true facts arranged as an excuse. The troops were deserting. Samuel had not come at the appointed time. The Philistines were gathering. And his reasoning, quoted in the text as his very thought, was this: "Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD." So I felt compelled, he said. I forced myself. Samuel's answer stripped the facts of their arrangement and named the act: "You have acted foolishly," Samuel declared. "You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you; if you had, the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time. But now your kingdom will not endure; the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people, because you have not kept the command of the LORD." A man after His own heart. The sentence is the first shadow of David, cast across Saul's reign while David is still an unknown shepherd boy years from Bethlehem's fields. Note what the crack was. It was not a lost battle or a moral scandal. It was the king reaching for the priest's office to save his position, taking, with liturgy, the one thing the warning in chapter 8 said kings take. Samuel went up to Gibeah and left him, and Saul counted what remained of the army that had numbered in the hundreds of thousands: about six hundred men. And the Philistines held the forges of the whole country, so that Israelite farmers sharpened their plowshares at Philistine smithies for a fee, and on the day of battle there was not a sword or a spear in Israel's ranks to be found, except two. Saul had one. Jonathan had the other.

title: Jonathan's Climb, and the Sentence on Saul
subtitle: 1 Samuel 14
description: Two men climb a cliff in faith, and a king spares what God devoted to destruction.
paragraphs: While Saul sat under the pomegranate tree at Migron with his six hundred men and his priest, his son walked out of the camp and did not tell him. Jonathan crossed toward the Philistine outpost at the pass of Michmash with one armor-bearer, two men total, into a defile with cliffs on both sides, and his reasoning for it is the theological high point of the reign: "Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will work on our behalf. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few." Perhaps. Nothing can hinder. Jonathan built no certainty into it, no claim on God, just an open door and a willingness to walk through it, and his armor-bearer answered with the loyalty the whole chapter runs on: "Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul." They agreed on a sign that put the outcome in the enemy's mouth. If the Philistines told them to wait, they would stay. If the Philistines called them up, that was the signal. The garrison, seeing two Hebrews crawl out of hiding, took the bait with a sneer: "Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes in which they were hiding!" And then: "Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!" Jonathan climbed the cliff on his hands and feet with his armor-bearer behind him, and the Philistines fell before them, about twenty men in the first assault on a scrap of ground, and then the panic did what two swords could not. It struck the whole Philistine host, camp and field and raiding parties, and the earth itself quaked, and the text names its source without blinking: the panic was from God.

Saul's watchmen saw the enemy army melting away. The roll was called and the king learned that the victory he was watching belonged to his absent son. He began a priestly consultation and then, as the noise of the rout grew, cut it off mid-rite: "Withdraw your hand." The army charged into a Philistine force already cutting itself apart, the Hebrew deserters in the Philistine camps switched sides, the men who had hidden in the hills came down and joined the pursuit, and the chapter delivers its verdict in words that leave no room for Saul's later version: "So the LORD saved Israel that day". Not Saul. Not even Jonathan, finally. The LORD, through two men who had said perhaps.

Now watch the king metabolize a victory he did not make. Before the day was out, Saul had bound the army under an oath with a curse in it: no food until evening, he said, "before I have taken vengeance on my enemies". My enemies. The vengeance had become personal property. The army, driven faint through a pursuit on empty stomachs, came into a forest where honey lay on the ground, and no one dared touch it except the one man who had not heard the oath. Jonathan dipped the end of his staff in the honeycomb, ate, "and his eyes brightened", and when a soldier explained the curse, the prince gave his father the review the courtiers would not: "My father has brought trouble to the land," Jonathan replied. "Just look at how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey. How much better it would have been if the troops had eaten freely today from the plunder they took from their enemies! Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been much greater?" By nightfall the starving troops fell on the spoil and ate meat with the blood still in it, a sin Saul had to stop with an improvised altar and slaughtering stones, and when he pushed for a night pursuit and finally consulted God properly, heaven answered with silence. No word at all.

Saul's response to the silence was an investigation, and the investigation was run by lot, and the lot worked its way down, past the whole army, past the king's house, to Jonathan. The confession was clean and it was brave: "I only tasted a little honey with the end of the staff that was in my hand. And now I must die?" Saul, who had sworn the oath, now swore to enforce it on his own son: "May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!" And here the book stages one of its great reversals of rank. The army, the same fainting, oath-bound army, stood between the king and the prince and overruled the king to his face, on theological grounds better than his: Jonathan had accomplished the great deliverance of the day, and "not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, for with God’s help he has accomplished this today". The people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die, and Saul accepted the overruling and went home. The victory chapter ends with the king's authority spent: his son alive by the army's verdict, his oath void, his pursuit abandoned.

The summary that follows says Saul fought successfully on every side for years, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zobah, Philistines, even Amalekites. Which is why the next mission matters so much: it came with instructions so explicit that partial obedience would have nowhere to hide. Samuel delivered them as a formal commission. Amalek was the ancient enemy, the nation that had fallen on Israel's stragglers on the way out of Egypt, and the sentence now pronounced reached back across the centuries: "Now go and attack the Amalekites and devote to destruction all that belongs to them. Do not spare them". The command went on to name the scope without exception, men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys, the whole herem, the devotion to destruction that removed a thing from human use entirely. Saul mustered two hundred ten thousand men. He did one thing honorably at the outset: he warned the Kenites, who had shown kindness to Israel in the Exodus, to separate themselves from Amalek, and they did. Then he struck the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur, and the book records the failure with an accountant's eye: "Saul and his troops spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else. They were unwilling to devote them to destruction, but they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless." The king of Amalek lived, a trophy. The best livestock lived, plunder. What died under the ban was everything nobody wanted anyway.

That night the word of the LORD came to Samuel with a sentence this series lets stand in its own words: "I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions." Samuel cried out to God all night, and went at dawn to confront a king who, he was told on the road, had stopped at Carmel to set up a monument to himself. Saul greeted the prophet with a blessing and a falsehood in the same breath: "May the LORD bless you. I have carried out the LORD’s instructions." And Samuel asked the question that has echoed down every century since, because the evidence was audible: "Then what is this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle that I hear?" Saul blamed the troops. The troops had spared the best animals, he said, for sacrifice, to the LORD your God. Listen to the pronouns Across both of his explanations, it is never our God or my God. It is your God, said twice to the prophet, as though the covenant were Samuel's private affair. Samuel cut him off and recited the king's own biography back to him: "Although you were once small in your own eyes, have you not become the head of the tribes of Israel?" The LORD anointed you, sent you, told you exactly what to do. Why did you not obey? Why did you rush on the plunder? Saul insisted once more that he had obeyed, that the troops had taken the animals for sacrifice at Gilgal, and Samuel answered with the oracle that stands at the center of this book and near the center of the whole Bible's teaching on worship: "Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obedience to His voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and arrogance is like the wickedness of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king."

Then, at last, Saul confessed, and even the confession carried its diagnosis inside it: "I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s commandment and your instructions, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice." Obedience was never his problem. He obeyed voices faithfully. The question was always which voice, the crowd's or God's, and on the two great tests of his reign he had chosen the crowd and called the choosing necessity. He begged Samuel to come back with him and worship, and Samuel refused, and turned to leave, and Saul grabbed at his robe and the hem tore, and Samuel read the tear as heaven's own handwriting: "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you." In the same conversation Samuel also said this, and the book leaves the two sayings standing side by side without a bridge: "Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind." God has regretted making Saul king, the chapter has already said twice, and God does not change His mind like a man. Samuel's point, in context, is a door closing: this sentence will not be negotiated, lobbied, or waited out. Saul's next words prove he heard only the public part of it. "I have sinned," Saul replied. "Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel. Come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD your God." Honor me before the elders. Samuel, for the people's sake and the day's, went back with him, and Saul worshiped. Then Samuel finished the mission himself, there at Gilgal, calling for Agag and pronouncing the measure-for-measure sentence over the king whose sword had emptied Israelite homes: "As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women." And Samuel went home to Ramah, and Saul went up to Gibeah, and they never met again in life. "And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul, and the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel."

title: The Shepherd Anointed, and the Giant
subtitle: 1 Samuel 16
description: A youngest son anointed in secret, and a shepherd who runs toward Goliath.
paragraphs: God let Samuel grieve for Saul, and then God ended the grieving. "How long are you going to mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself." A king for Myself. Israel had demanded a king for themselves, and gotten one built to their specifications; the replacement would be God's own selection, made by God's own criteria, and almost nobody would know it had happened. Samuel's first response shows what Saul's Israel had already become: the prophet was afraid the king would kill him for going. He went under the cover of a sacrifice, and the elders of Bethlehem came out trembling to meet him, because in Saul's kingdom a visit from Samuel might be an arrest: "Do you come in peace?"

At Jesse's house the sons were paraded, and the first of them walked in tall and broad and king-shaped, and Samuel, the man who had watched God reject a king chosen for his height, made Israel's mistake all over again on sight: "Surely here before the LORD is His anointed." God's correction of His own prophet is the interpretive key to both books of Samuel, and it names the disqualifier directly: "Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart." Height. Saul had been chosen by a nation measuring from the head up, a head taller than everyone, and the new king would be measured from the heart out. Six more sons passed. Seven rejections. "The LORD has not chosen any of these." Samuel asked the question that exposed how the youngest son ranked in his own father's house: "Are these all the sons you have?" And Jesse answered almost as an afterthought: "There is still the youngest," he said, "but he is tending the sheep." Not summoned. Not named by his father in the text, just the youngest, out with the flock, an errand boy's absence at a sacrifice where kings were being chosen. Samuel made the whole feast stand waiting: we will not sit down until he arrives. They sent for him, and the shepherd came in from the fields, "ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance", and the LORD said the words the whole secret turned on: "Rise and anoint him, for he is the one." Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed David in front of the brothers who had all been passed over, "and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward".

The next verse performs the transfer in a single breath: "Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him." The book states the exchange flatly, Spirit for spirit, and does not soften its own attribution; the torment that now stalked Saul is laid at heaven's door by the same narrator who credits heaven with David's rise. Saul's servants prescribed music, and the search for a harpist produced a courtier's description of the new servant that reads, in hindsight, like a dossier: Jesse's son "knows how to play the harp. He is a mighty man of valor, a warrior, eloquent and handsome, and the LORD is with him." Mighty man of valor, warrior, the LORD with him: all of it already true of the shepherd before Goliath, filed away in small talk. Saul sent for David, and Saul loved him, the text says, very much, and made him his armor-bearer, and whenever the distress came on the king, the boy from Bethlehem played, "and the spirit of distress would depart from him". The rejected king's only relief was the anointed king's hands.

Then the Philistines came back, and the story doubles around to introduce David a second time, from the sheep side, as though the court musician were another person, and both portraits are left standing. In the Valley of Elah the armies camped on facing hills, and out of the Philistine lines came a champion whose measurements the text gives like a quartermaster: Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span tall, nearer ten feet than nine, a bronze helmet, a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, a spear shaft like a weaver's beam with a six-hundred-shekel iron head. Twice a day, for forty days, he stood in the valley and offered single combat with national stakes, winner's nation enslaved to the loser's, and ended with a line aimed past the soldiers at their God: "I defy the ranks of Israel this day! Give me a man to fight!" And the king who was a head taller than any man in Israel, and his whole army, "were dismayed and greatly afraid".

David arrived on an errand. Jesse sent him with roasted grain and loaves for his three oldest brothers and ten cheeses for their commander, and the boy left the sheep with a keeper, reached the camp as the army marched out shouting, dumped his supplies with the quartermaster, and ran to the battle line, and arrived just in time to hear the morning taunt delivered again. What he asked the soldiers around him shows where his mind went that theirs had not. They talked about the king's reward, riches and the princess and tax exemption. David asked about the insult: "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" His oldest brother heard him and lit into him in front of the men, the rejected Eliab accusing the anointed David of the exact charge God had cleared him of: "I know your pride and wickedness of heart", he said, you came down to watch the battle. David's answer was the sound of a younger brother who had been absorbing this for years: "What have I done now?" But other ears carried his words to Saul, and Saul sent for him, and the shepherd told the king of Israel what no soldier in the valley had dared to say: "Let no man’s heart fail on account of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him!"

Saul objected with the resume gap, a boy against a warrior from his youth, and David answered with the only credentials he had, from the years nobody had watched: the lion and the bear that came for the flock, chased down and killed by hand, lambs rescued out of their mouths. "Your servant has killed lions and bears; this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God." And then the creed underneath the credentials: "The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." Past deliverance read as future promise. Saul gave him permission and his own armor, and the armor did not fit the boy's habits, and David took it off and went down to the brook and chose five smooth stones and walked toward the Philistine with a staff, a sling, and a shepherd's bag. Goliath saw him coming and was insulted to the bottom of his giant heart: "Am I a dog," he said, "that you come at me with sticks?" and he cursed David by his gods and promised his flesh to the birds.

David answered the curse with the longest speech anyone gives in the chapter, and it is not about David. "You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied." This day, he said, the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and the Philistine army's carcasses to the birds, "Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel. And all those assembled here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and He will give all of you into our hands." It is Jonathan's theology with a sling in it, the same confession his father's son made on the cliff at Michmash: the LORD saves, by many or by few, and the instruments are interchangeable. Then David did the thing that separates him from the king on the hill. Goliath moved forward to attack, and David ran. Toward him. He ran quickly to the battle line, hand in the bag, stone in the sling, and the stone sank into the giant's forehead, "and he fell facedown on the ground", face down in the dirt of the valley like Dagon on his temple floor before the ark. David had brought no sword, so he finished it with the Philistine's own, taking the head with the giant's blade, and the Philistine army ran, and Israel and Judah charged shouting and cut them down along the road to the very gates of Gath and Ekron. David carried the head to Jerusalem and kept the armor in his tent, a shepherd rearranging the furniture of the future.

And on the hill, the king who had loved the harpist, who had made him armor-bearer, who had sent him down in his own tunic, watched the boy come back holding the giant's head, and asked his general the question the rest of the book exists to answer: "Abner, whose son is this young man?" Abner did not know. So the king had him brought in, head still in hand, and asked him directly, and David answered with the plain address of the house God had chosen over Saul's: "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem".

title: Ten Thousands, and the Son of the King
subtitle: 1 Samuel 18
description: A victory song, three spears, a covenant, and arrows by the stone Ezel.
paragraphs: The first person in Saul's house to see David clearly was Saul's heir. After the giant, David finished speaking with the king, and the text says the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, "and Jonathan loved him as himself". What the crown prince did next can be read as friendship, and it can also be read as abdication performed in clothing. Jonathan made a covenant with David, and stripped off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, "along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt". The prince's robe. The prince's weapons. Whether Jonathan understood the full transfer he was enacting, the narrator lays the garments out one by one and lets them preach: the son of Saul handed the future to the son of Jesse, and loved him while he did it. Saul, meanwhile, kept David at court permanently, and sent him out on campaign after campaign, and David prospered at everything, and it pleased the people, and it pleased Saul's own officers.

Then the army came home and the women of Israel sang the king into his obsession. Out of every city they poured with tambourines and dancing to meet the returning troops, and their song was a comparison, because victory songs always are: "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands." Saul heard arithmetic, and the arithmetic had a remainder. "They have ascribed tens of thousands to David," he said, "but only thousands to me. What more can he have but the kingdom?" It is the most lucid sentence he speaks in his decline. He was not wrong about the trajectory; he was wrong about the response, which was murder. "And from that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David." The next day the distressing spirit came on the king while David played the harp, and Saul, spear in hand, hurled it twice at the musician, thinking, the narrator says, to pin him to the wall. Twice David slipped it. And the fear underneath the jealousy is named in words that summarize the whole transfer: Saul was afraid of David, "because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul".

So Saul tried distance as a weapon. He gave David a command of a thousand and sent him out to the wars, which was exposure strategy, sending the rival where spears were thickest, and it backfired completely, because David kept winning, and "all Israel and Judah loved David, because he was leading them out to battle and back". Then Saul tried family. He offered his older daughter Merab for the bride-price of valor in the LORD's battles, thinking the Philistines would do his killing for him, and when the time came he gave Merab to another man instead. His younger daughter Michal loved David, and Saul heard that with pleasure, because a king's daughter could be set as a snare. The dowry he demanded was designed to be fatal: no gold, just a hundred Philistine foreskins, proof of a hundred kills up close. David went out before the deadline and brought back two hundred. Saul gave him Michal, and the chapter's accounting closes on the king like a cell door: when Saul saw "that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved David", he was afraid all the more: "So from then on Saul was David’s enemy."

The attempts now became orders. Saul commanded Jonathan and all his servants to kill David, and Jonathan, who had everything to lose by it, warned David and then stood before his father and argued the case on the facts: "He took his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced, so why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David for no reason?" It worked. Saul swore an oath by the LORD that David would not be put to death, and David returned to court as before. It did not hold. War came, David won again, the spirit came again, and the spear came a third time while the harp played, and this time David fled into the night and did not come back. Saul sent men to watch his house and kill him at dawn, and Michal lowered him from the window and laid a household idol in his bed with goat hair at its head to buy him the dark hours. When the messengers finally forced the room, they found the idol, and Saul's order to the second squad tells you how far the oath had rotted: "Bring him up to me in his bed so I can kill him." The psalm Israel still sings about that night of watching and escape is Psalm 59, whose heading ties it to this very errand; the book leaves the song to the Psalter and keeps its camera on the flight. David ran to the one address left to him: Samuel, at Ramah, the rejected prophet who had anointed him, and told him everything.

What happened at Ramah is the strangest protective custody in the Bible. Saul sent messengers to Naioth to seize David, and they found Samuel presiding over a company of prophets prophesying, and the Spirit of God fell on the arrest squad and they prophesied too. A second squad: the same. A third squad: the same. So Saul went himself, and the Spirit came on him on the road and he prophesied the whole way to Naioth, and there the king of Israel stripped off his robes and prophesied before Samuel and collapsed naked on the ground for a day and a night, while his quarry stood safe a few feet away. The proverb coined in wonder on the day of his anointing was quoted again, and the second time it is an obituary for his dignity: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" The God who would not let Saul's spears land would not let his errands land either.

David still could not believe the breach was final, which is why the last of these three chapters belongs to the arrows. He came to Jonathan with the question innocence asks power: "What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?" And then the plainest self-assessment in his story: "there is but a step between me and death". Jonathan promised the sentence that defined him: "Whatever you desire, I will do for you." They built a test around the New Moon feast. David's seat would be empty; Jonathan would offer the Bethlehem excuse; the king's temperature would tell the truth. And before they parted, Jonathan renewed the covenant, and this time he aimed it past David at the future, at a throne he would never sit on: "And as long as I live, treat me with the LORD’s loving devotion, that I may not die, and do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household". He set the term himself, at the far end of the revolution: "when the LORD cuts off every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth." The prince was asking the shepherd to spare the prince's children after the revolution. David swore it. The word is hesed again, loyal kindness, the word that carried Ruth's book, passing now between the heir who would lose the kingdom and the shepherd who would gain it.

At the feast, the empty seat passed one day unremarked. On the second day Saul asked after him, and Jonathan delivered the excuse, and the king exploded at his own son with a fury that laid the whole dynasty bare: "You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame and to the shame of the mother who bore you? For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established." The math was exact and Saul knew it: David alive meant Jonathan dispossessed. When Jonathan demanded what David had done to deserve death, Saul threw his spear at his own heir. The prince left the table in fierce anger, eating nothing, grieving, the text says, over his father's shameful treatment of David. In the morning he went to the field and shot his arrows past the stone Ezel, and called to the boy the words that were really for the man hiding behind the stone: "Isn’t the arrow beyond you?" And then, with an urgency the boy could not understand: "Hurry! Make haste! Do not delay!" The boy gathered the arrows and went back to the city, and David came out of hiding and fell facedown and bowed three times, and the two of them wept together, and the text says David wept the more. Jonathan sent him away with the covenant as their last word, the promise they had sworn between themselves and their descendants: "May the LORD be a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever." Then David departed, a fugitive now for the rest of Saul's reign, and Jonathan went back into the city, to his father's table, to eat beside the man who had thrown a spear at him, carrying a secret that would outlive them both.

title: The Fugitive
subtitle: 1 Samuel 21
description: Nob, Gath, the cave of Adullam, and a king spared in the dark at En-gedi.
paragraphs: David's first stop as a fugitive was a sanctuary, and he arrived lying. At Nob, the priest Ahimelech met him trembling, because royal servants did not travel alone, and David explained that he was on a secret mission for the king, that his men were waiting at an appointed place, and that he needed bread. There was no mission. There were no men. The story got him what he needed anyway: the only bread in the house, the consecrated loaves, the Bread of the Presence, given to a hungry fugitive by a priest who bent the rules of holiness toward mercy. It also got him a sword, and the sword was an old friend. Behind the ephod, wrapped in a cloth, Nob kept the trophy of the Valley of Elah, and the priest offered it and David said the obvious: "There is none like it; give it to me." One man watched the whole transaction and remembered it, a herdsman detained at the sanctuary that day: Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief shepherd. David saw him there. File it the way David did, with a weight that will matter: he noticed Doeg, and went on eating.

From Nob he ran to the last address anyone would choose, Gath, Goliath's hometown, carrying Goliath's sword, and Achish's courtiers recognized him by the song: was this not David, the king of the land, the tens of thousands man? David, who had faced the giant without blinking, came apart at being recognized, and saved himself by an act. He feigned madness before the court, scratching at the gate doors, letting spittle run down his beard, until Achish drove him out with contempt: "Am I in need of madmen, that you have brought this man to rave in my presence? Must this man come into my house?" Israel sings two psalms out of that humiliation to this day: Psalm 56, whose heading names David's seizure by the Philistines in Gath, and Psalm 34, whose heading ties his feigned madness and escape to the song of a man who blessed the LORD at all times for it. The book does not quote them; it just leaves the drooling fugitive at the gate, and lets the Psalter tell you what he was praying.

At the cave of Adullam the fugitive became a captain. His brothers and his father's whole household came down to him, and then came everybody with nowhere else to go: "And all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him." The cave filled with the casualties of Saul's kingdom, and David's first royal act was elder care. He took his parents across to Moab, to the king of his great-grandmother Ruth's people, and asked shelter for them "until I learn what God will do for me". Then the prophet Gad told him not to stay in the stronghold but to go back into Judah, into the danger, and David obeyed. Note what the wilderness court was accumulating while the palace emptied: a prophet to guide him, and presently a priest with the ephod to inquire for him. Saul, who had lost Samuel, was about to ensure he had no priests either.

At Gibeah, the king sat under his tamarisk tree with his spear in his hand and harangued his own tribe like a man reading his fears aloud. "Is the son of Jesse giving all of you fields and vineyards and making you commanders of thousands or hundreds?" It was Samuel's warning turned inside out: the king who took everyone's fields accused the fugitive of promising fields. You have all conspired against me, Saul said; not one of you told me my own son made a covenant with him. And into the silence of the Benjaminites stepped the one man at court with no Israelite loyalties to lose. Doeg the Edomite reported Nob: "I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob." He inquired of God for him, gave him provisions, gave him Goliath's sword. Ahimelech was summoned with his whole father's house, and his defense, delivered to a king holding a spear, is a model of a clear conscience: "Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, the captain of your bodyguard and honored in your house?" I inquired for him as I had always done; I knew nothing of any affair. Saul sentenced them anyway: "You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house!" And here the court split along the line of the whole book. The king's Israelite guards, ordered to kill the priests of the LORD, refused outright; they would not lift a hand. So Saul turned to the Edomite: "You turn and strike down the priests!" Doeg did. Eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod died that day, and Doeg went on to Nob and put the city to the sword, men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep: the full catalogue of destruction, word for word the ban Saul had refused to complete against Amalek, executed instead against a town of priests inside Israel. Psalm 52 carries Doeg's name in its heading forever, David's verdict on the informer set to music.

One priest survived. Abiathar, Ahimelech's son, escaped and ran to David, and David took the guilt on himself in words nobody made him say: "I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul. I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house." Stay with me, he said; the man seeking your life is seeking mine; "You will be safe with me". It is the covenant instinct of David in one scene, absorbing blame and offering shelter, and from that day the fugitive's camp had what Saul's palace lacked, a priest of the LORD with the ephod of inquiry, because Saul had murdered the rest.

The inquiries saved more than David. When the Philistines raided Keilah, a walled town of Judah, David asked the LORD twice, over his own men's fear, and went and saved the city whose king-protector should have saved it. Saul heard David was shut inside walls and read the trap as God's gift: "God has delivered him into my hand, for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars." David asked the ephod two questions, and the answers describe his whole fugitive life in advance. Will Saul come down? He will. Will the citizens of Keilah, the people David had just rescued, surrender him to Saul? They will. Gratitude had a shelf life of days; David slipped out before the siege, six hundred men now, and lived place to place in the wilderness of Ziph, where the text posts its quiet verdict across the whole era: "Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand."

In that wilderness the covenant came to him one more time in person. Jonathan slipped out of his father's court to Horesh and strengthened David's hand in God, and the prince spoke the succession aloud, from the far side of surrender: "Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you. And you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command. Even my father Saul knows this is true." They renewed the covenant, and Jonathan went home. The Ziphites, David's own Judeans, then did what Keilah had only been predicted to do: they went up to Gibeah and sold his position to Saul, and Saul blessed them for it in the LORD's name: "May you be blessed by the LORD," replied Saul, "for you have had compassion on me." Psalm 54's heading remembers the Ziphites' errand. Twice Saul's net closed on the mountain in Maon, his men on one slope, David's on the other, the trap an hour from springing, and twice or once was enough: a messenger galloped in with news of a Philistine raid, and Saul had to break off and go defend the kingdom he was neglecting to chase the man he feared. The place got a name out of it, the Rock of Escape.

Then, at En-gedi, the hunt delivered Saul himself into David's hand, helpless and alone. The king came into a cave to relieve himself, the very cave in whose recesses David and his men were hiding, and David's men read it as heaven's signature on regicide, quoting what they took for a prophecy: "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish." David crept forward through the dark with a knife, close enough to kill the king of Israel unhurried, and cut off a corner of his robe instead. Even that much violence against the anointed man's clothing stricken his conscience afterward, and he held his men back with both hands and a doctrine: "The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD’s anointed. May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." Saul had been anointed by Samuel; the office was God's, and David would not take the kingdom out of God's timing with a blade, not even in self-defense, not even with opportunity served up in a cave.

From the cave mouth he called after the departing king, bowed facedown, and made his case with the evidence in his hand: "See, my father, look at the corner of your robe in my hand. For I cut it off, but I did not kill you." And he put the feud in the court where he had decided it belonged: "May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you." Against whom has the king of Israel come out, he asked; you are pursuing a dead dog, a flea. And Saul, confronted with mercy at point-blank range, broke, and wept aloud, and said the truest things he ever said about the two of them: "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." And then the hunter prophesied against his own hunt: "Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." He asked one thing, the thing Jonathan had asked, that David swear not to cut off his descendants or wipe out his name when he came to power, and David swore it freely. Then Saul went home. And David, who had just heard his enemy confess his destiny and weep over him, did not go home with him, and did not trust the tears past the horizon. He went back up to the stronghold. Both men, for once, understood each other perfectly.

title: Abigail, and the Night at Endor
subtitle: 1 Samuel 25
description: A wise woman stops a massacre, a spear taken twice, and a king's last night at Endor.
paragraphs: The book pauses on a death before it resumes the chase. "When Samuel died, all Israel gathered to mourn for him; and they buried him at his home in Ramah." The prophet who had anointed both kings was gone, and with him went the last voice Saul had ever obeyed, even badly. David withdrew to the wilderness of Paran, where his six hundred were doing for local shepherds what an army does in a country the king has abandoned: guarding them. In Carmel lived the richest beneficiary of that protection, a Calebite named Nabal, three thousand sheep, a thousand goats, and a wife named Abigail, whom the text introduces in a single balanced sentence against her husband: she was intelligent and beautiful; he was harsh and evil in his dealings. At shearing time, the feast of the pastoral year, David sent ten men with a courteous request for whatever Nabal could spare, pointing out, accurately, that his shepherds had lost nothing while David's men were near. Nabal answered the courtesy with a sneer that hit every target at once, David's legitimacy, David's family, and David's men: "Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse? Many servants these days are breaking away from their masters. Why should I take my bread and water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, and give them to these men whose origin I do not know?"

David's response shows how thin the fugitive's righteousness could wear under insult. He did not appeal to God or weigh the provocation. He swore an oath of extermination: "May God punish David, and ever so severely, if I let one male belonging to Nabal survive until morning." Four hundred men strapped on swords to massacre a household over an unpaid catering bill and a rude answer. What saved David from the worst act of his life was a servant's report and a wife's speed. One of Nabal's own young men told Abigail what her husband had done and what was coming, and his testimony about David's men is in the record: "They were a wall around us, both day and night, the whole time we were herding our sheep near them." Abigail loaded donkeys with a small harvest of food, two hundred loaves, wine, dressed sheep, roasted grain, raisins, fig cakes, and rode out into the ravine to meet four hundred armed men, without telling her husband. She came off the donkey and fell facedown and delivered the greatest speech of the fugitive years, beginning by absorbing the guilt herself: "My lord, may the blame be on me alone". Then she separated her husband from his household with the text's own dictionary: "My lord should pay no attention to this scoundrel Nabal, for he lives up to his name: His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him."

Then she did the thing no one else in this book manages with David. She prophesied at him, accurately, and used his future as the argument against his present. The LORD, she said, has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand. Your enemies will end like Nabal. "Please forgive your servant’s offense, for the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles." And the lives of your enemies, she said, God "shall fling away the lives of your enemies like stones from a sling", a weapon David of all men could picture. Her closing argument was aimed at his conscience years ahead of schedule: when the LORD has made you ruler, "then my lord will have no remorse or guilt of conscience over needless bloodshed and revenge. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, may you remember your servant." She was asking a man marching to a massacre to imagine himself a king looking back at this morning, and to choose the memory he could live with.

David stood down, completely, in words that show why he and Saul are different men. Saul, corrected, negotiated for appearances; David, corrected by the wife of the man he came to kill, blessed the correction itself: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day! Blessed is your discernment, and blessed are you, because today you kept me from bloodshed and from avenging myself by my own hand." Had you not hurried, he told her, not one male of Nabal's house would have survived the night. He took the food, sent her home in peace, and let the vengeance go to the address Abigail had assigned it. That night Nabal held a feast fit for a king in his house, the king's courtesy he had refused the future king's men, and got very drunk, and in the morning his wife told him everything, and his heart failed within him and he became like a stone, and about ten days later the LORD struck him dead. David heard, and read the whole affair as God's own court ruling: "Blessed be the LORD, who has upheld my cause against the reproach of Nabal and has restrained His servant from evil." Then he sent for Abigail and married the woman who had saved him from himself. The chapter's final verse is Saul's counterstroke from far away: he had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to another man, erasing the marriage as a king erases a contract.

The Ziphites sold David's position again, and Saul came down with three thousand men again, and the pattern of En-gedi repeated itself one valley over, sharpened. David and Abishai walked into the sleeping camp at night and stood over the king, his spear stuck in the ground by his head, his general and army asleep around him in a sleep the text credits to the LORD. Abishai asked for the kill with a professional's economy: "Today God has delivered your enemy into your hand. Now, therefore, please let me thrust the spear through him into the ground with one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice!" David refused, and this time the refusal comes out as settled doctrine with a timetable attached: "Do not destroy him, for who can extend a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?" And then, over the sleeping king, David pronounced the manner of Saul's death without knowing he was doing it: "As surely as the LORD lives, the LORD Himself will strike him down; either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish." He took the spear and the water jug and crossed the gulf, and shouted the guard awake and shamed Abner for sleeping on duty, and Saul, hearing the voice, said what he always said in these encounters: "Is that your voice, David my son?"

David's answer this time carries the deepest complaint of his exile. Why does my lord pursue his servant? What evil is in my hand? If the LORD has stirred you up, let Him accept an offering; but if men have done it, may they be cursed: "For today they have driven me away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD", telling me, in effect, "Go, serve other gods". The king of Israel, he said, "has come out to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains". And Saul confessed more honestly than he ever had: "I have sinned.
