Come back, David my son. I will never harm you again, because today you considered my life precious. I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!" It is, in content, an abdication of the quarrel, and Saul sealed it with a blessing that reads like a last will: "May you be blessed, David my son. You will accomplish great things and will surely prevail." They are the last words the two men ever exchanged. David went on his way. He did not come back. The reconciliation was real at the level of Saul's feeling and worthless at the level of Saul's behavior, and David had learned to price it accordingly.

Because even David's faith had a fatigue limit, and the next chapter opens inside his head at its lowest ebb: "One of these days now I will be swept away by the hand of Saul." No inquiry of the LORD is recorded this time, no ephod, just a tired man's arithmetic: the best move left was out, to Philistia, to the protection of Israel's enemy. Achish of Gath, who had once expelled him as a madman, now received him as a defector with six hundred families, and gave him a town of his own, Ziklag, which belonged to Judah's kings from that day forward. For a year and four months David lived the double life, raiding Israel's desert enemies, the Geshurites and Amalekites of the south, and reporting to Achish that he had raided Judah, leaving no survivors behind him to correct the story. The text records the arrangement without comment, the anointed of God surviving inside the enemy's patronage on managed truth, and Achish, entirely deceived, concluded that David had made himself an utter stench to his own people and would be his servant forever.

Then the Philistines mustered for the great campaign, and Achish summoned his vassal with an honor that was a trap in itself: David and his men would march with him against Israel, and David would be his bodyguard for life. David's answer deserves to be heard with both its meanings at once, because the text declines to choose between them: "Then you will come to know what your servant can do." The Philistine war machine was assembling at Shunem, and Israel camped opposite on Gilboa, and Saul saw the size of the army and his heart trembled violently, and he inquired of the LORD, and the heavens he had spent years disobeying went completely silent. "He inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets." Dreams, the priestly lot, the prophets: all three channels, closed in one verse, and each of them closed by Saul's own history. He had slaughtered the priests of the Urim. He had driven out and lost the prophets. Samuel was dead.

So the king who had purged the land of mediums went looking for one. His servants knew of a woman at Endor who still practiced, and Saul disguised himself and came to her by night with two men, and asked her to consult a spirit and bring up the one he would name. The woman, no fool, quoted the law at the stranger: you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums; why are you setting a trap for my life? And the king swore to her, by the LORD, the very God whose law he was breaking, that no punishment would come on her for this. Then he named the name: "Bring up Samuel," he said. What happened next frightened even the professional. When the woman saw Samuel, she screamed, because she understood instantly who her client was: "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!" The book tells the scene as it stands in the text, without explaining the machinery. She described what she saw: "I see a god coming up out of the earth," an old man wrapped in a robe, and Saul knew it was Samuel and bowed with his face to the ground. And the voice that spoke was the voice that had pronounced every sentence of his reign, annoyed at being summoned: "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul poured out the whole of it: "I am deeply distressed," he said. "The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do."

The answer was the old sentence, unchanged, plus an appointment. "Why do you consult me," asked Samuel, "since the LORD has turned away from you and become your enemy?" The LORD has done what He said through me: "The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor David. Because you did not obey the LORD or carry out His burning anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today." Amalek. From beyond death, the prophet traced the fall to the same altar at Gilgal where it had begun. And then the final word, the one the night had been purchased for: "Moreover, the LORD will deliver Israel with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me." Tomorrow. Saul fell full length on the ground, emptied of strength; he had eaten nothing all day and night. And the last kindness Saul received in this world came from the woman of Endor, who had risked her life at his word and now insisted the condemned king eat: she killed her fattened calf, baked unleavened bread with her own hands, and set a meal before him and his servants, and they ate, and rose, and went out into the night, back toward Gilboa, where tomorrow was waiting.

title: Ziklag in Ashes, and the Fall of Saul
subtitle: 1 Samuel 29
description: Everything lost and recovered at Ziklag, and the death of Saul and Jonathan on Gilboa.
paragraphs: The Philistine army reviewed at Aphek with David marching in it, at the rear, behind Achish, six hundred Israelites in the ranks of Israel's enemy, on their way to fight Israel. It was the trap his whole double life had been building toward, and it was sprung not by God and not by Saul but by the Philistine high command, who looked at the Hebrew contingent and refused it. What about these Hebrews? they demanded, and Achish defended his vassal with an oath that lands strangely from a Philistine king: "As surely as the LORD lives, you have been upright, and it seems right in my sight that you should march in and out with me in the army, because I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until this day." The commanders were unmoved. They quoted Israel's own victory song back at him, the one about the thousands and the tens of thousands, and asked the practical question: what better way for this man to regain his master's favor than with the heads of Philistine soldiers? Send him back. Achish, outvoted, apologized to David in terms no Israelite had used about him in years: "I know that you are as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God." David protested his dismissal in form, asking what fault had been found in him, to keep him "from going along to fight against the enemies of my lord the king", and then he got up before dawn and marched home to Ziklag, out of the war entirely. The book never says what David would have done on the field at Gilboa had he stayed. It simply removes him, by enemy distrust, from the possibility, and lets his dismissal preach: the commanders of the Philistines built the wall that kept God's anointed from raising a sword against God's people.

Three days' march brought his men home to a smoking ruin. While David had been reviewing at Aphek, Amalek had come up from the south, the same people Saul had once been sent to destroy and had half-destroyed, and had raided Ziklag in its emptiness, burned it, and carried off everyone in it, the women and children of all six hundred families. They had killed no one; the text buries that mercy in a subordinate clause, and it is the hinge the whole rescue hangs on. David and his men came into the ashes and found the town burned and their wives and sons and daughters gone, and they "lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep". Both of David's wives were among the captives. And when the weeping spent itself it turned to the politics of grief: the men, every one of them bereaved, began to speak of stoning David, the leader whose alliance had left the town uncovered and whose families were suffering for it. It is the lowest sentence of his life in this book, lower than the cave, lower than the madman's drool at Gath, and the book sets against it one line that has steadied readers ever since: "But David found strength in the LORD his God." He did not argue with the men, organize, or despair. He called for the ephod. The fugitive years had taught him the sequence his despair at Ziklag's founding had skipped: ask first. "Should I pursue these raiders? Will I overtake them?" "Pursue them," the LORD replied, "for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives."

At the Brook of Besor, two hundred of his six hundred were too exhausted to cross, and David left them with the supplies and went on with four hundred, and the story bends toward one of its gentlest details. On the way they found an Egyptian half dead in a field, a slave abandoned by his Amalekite master when he fell sick, and David's men, hunting a raiding party on a promise, stopped and fed him, bread and fig cake and raisins and water, three days' worth of hunger answered before a single question was asked. Revived, he told them everything: he had been on the raid; he knew where the raiders were; on an oath that David would neither kill him nor return him to his master, he would lead them there. He led them down at twilight onto the whole Amalekite force spread out over the land, eating and drinking and dancing over the plunder of two countries, and David struck them from twilight until the evening of the next day, and four hundred young men on camels were all that escaped. And the recovery was total, and the text totals it like a man counting children: "So David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives. Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken. David brought everything back."

Then the plunder nearly started a civil war inside his own camp. The men who had fought wanted the recovered goods kept among the fighters; the two hundred who had stayed at Besor should get their families and nothing more. The speakers are named by the narrator with an old word, the wicked and worthless men, and David overruled them with a ruling he made statute in Israel for good: "My brothers, you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us. Who will listen to your proposal? The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike." The man who would not take Saul's life by the sword also would not let victory become prize money. Grace, distributed by rule. And out of the surplus he sent gifts ahead of him to the elders of Judah, town by town, Bethel and Ramoth and Jattir and Hebron and all the places he had roamed, saying, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies." The fugitive was doing the work of a king in Judah while the king was still on his throne.

In those same days, the army David had been dismissed from met the Philistines at Mount Gilboa, and the word spoken at Endor kept its appointment. The men of Israel fled, and many fell, and the Philistines closed on the royal family: "The Philistines hotly pursued Saul and his sons, and they killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua." Jonathan died first in the list, as he had lived: beside his father, in the war his father had made, the finest man of the reign buried in its wreckage. The archers found Saul and wounded him badly, and the king's last command was to his armor-bearer: "Draw your sword and run me through with it, or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and torture me!" The young man refused, terrified, and Saul took his own sword and fell on it, and the armor-bearer fell on his beside him. "So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day." Tomorrow, Samuel had said, you and your sons will be with me. The cities of the valley emptied at the news, and the Philistines moved into Israelite houses.

The next day they came to strip the dead and found the king, and they treated his body as his kingdom had taught them trophies were treated. They cut off his head and sent it with his armor through the land as a proclamation in the temples of their idols; the armor they displayed in the temple of the Ashtoreths, and his body they fastened to the wall of Beth-shan. It is the scene from the ark's captivity played in reverse: Israel's anointed hung as a Philistine trophy, and this time no god fell on his face in the night. But the book's first debt was still outstanding, and it was collected by the town that owed it. When the men of Jabesh-gilead heard what had been done to Saul, the town Saul had rescued in his first and finest campaign, the town of the gouged eyes and the dawn deliverance, their men of valor marched all night, took the bodies of Saul and his sons down from the wall, brought them home to Jabesh, burned them there, buried the bones under the tamarisk tree, and fasted seven days. The book ends there, in Jabesh, with the first king of Israel buried by the first people he saved, mourned properly by the only town that never forgot him.

What David did when the news reached Ziklag, and the song he sang over Saul and Jonathan, the book of Samuel holds for its second half, where it belongs. This book closes on the burial mound and the empty throne, with the word of the LORD having fallen nowhere: everything Samuel spoke from the night God called the boy had come to pass, down to the day. And in Bethlehem's line, still carrying Amalek's plunder as gifts to Judah's elders, the man after God's own heart was waiting, as he had waited in caves and courts for a decade, for the kingdom to come to him the way the anointing had: from God's hand, at God's time, with his own hands kept clean of the taking.
